|---|---|
| `index` | the module's id within its link unit, from zero |
| `name` | the path below the C root of its translation unit, or of its header for a header module |
| `status` | `todo` or `frozen`; see [Status](#2-status) |
| `foundational` | `true` for a foundational module, `false` otherwise; see `decomposition`'s Foundational modules section |
| `depends_on` | an array of dependency records; see [Dependencies](#8-link_unitsmodulesdepends_on) |
| `translation_unit` | the module's TU, as a [file entry](#5-file-entries); `null` for a header module |
| `internal_headers` | the headers the build does not install that the module defines items in, as file entries |
| `api_headers` | the headers the build installs that the module defines or declares items in, as file entries |
| `tests` | the test files tied to the module, those whose subject it is, as file entries whose `items` select test functions; see [File entries](#5-file-entries) |
| `objective` | the translation intent recorded for this module |

|---|---|

Test files are not owned: a test file is listed in the `tests` of every module it is

---
name: schedule-schema
description: "The fields of schedule.json: modules, waves, items, batches, progress, indices and re-planning. Read before writing or reading schedule.json."
---

# schedule.json schema

Field meaning for `<workdir>/crustify/artifacts/schedule.json`, the campaign's module
order, waves and batches. Layout examples: [`templates/schedule.json`](../../../templates/schedule.json), and a port
campaign's, [`templates/schedule.port.json`](../../../templates/schedule.port.json).

The campaign has one schedule, which every planner run extends: the first run creates it,
and each later one appends the waves its scope adds and re-plans the waves that have not
started. Waves are computable in advance, so writing them down makes a campaign's shape
reviewable before it spends anything; their batches are not, since they are packed when
each wave starts, as `scheduling`'s Batches section describes.

An audit's review waves are not recorded in it.

The schedule holds two kinds of field:

- the plan: the order of the modules, the waves, their dependencies and their items,
  decided by planning; and
- the progress: each wave's `status` and `packed_with`, and its `batches`, each with its
  worklist, `status` and `commits`, recorded as the work launches and lands.

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `schema_version` | `6` |
| `modules` | the order of the campaign's modules, one record per module the schedule holds waves of, by `layer` |
| `waves` | the campaign's waves, in `index` order |

## 1. modules[*]

The order of the modules is computed over every module of the decomposition, as
`scheduling`'s Order section describes, and recorded here, with the
dependencies it keeps and those it cuts.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `link_unit`, `module`, `foundational` | the module's identity in `modules.json`, as its `link_units[*].name`, its `name` and its `foundational` |
| `layer` | its place in the order of the modules: 0 for one that depends on no module ordered before it, else one more than the highest of those it depends on |
| `waves` | the indices of its waves |
| `depends_on.scheduled` | the modules it depends on that are ordered before it, each a dependency record below |
| `depends_on.cut` | the modules it depends on that are ordered after it, its dependency on them cut to break a cycle, each a dependency record with its `items` |
| `depends_on.external` | the out-of-tree libraries its units use, each an out-of-tree record below |

A dependency record names the module depended on, by `link_unit`, `module` and
`foundational`, and counts what this module's units use of it:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `unique_edges` | the distinct units of that module they use: one binding each, when the dependency is cut |
| `total_edges` | every unit edge from this module's units to that module's |

promoted. A wave `packed_with` another has no batches of its own: its `status` follows

be packed again into new batches, which take the next free indices, and review batches are
added as the batches they review land, as `reviewing` describes. A

their homes there, as `scheduling`'s Wrap batches section describes.

landing. An item's status is that of the batch that holds it: a planned item is translated

promotion fast-forwards without rewriting them.

## 4. Indices

A started wave's `index` is its permanent id: its branch, the batch ids
`wave-<index>/batch-<index>` and the run dirs are named from it, so it is never reused,
renumbered or moved, and they keep identifying the same work.

reviews dir, as `layout` spells them, each run's `task.json` naming the batch's wave and
index.

commit 25b3fe2d0a8c51d0c2b4f1f95d95b4a7f71de379
Author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>
Date:   Fri Nov 13 18:12:04 2026 +0000

    crustify: plan FILE, fprintf and stderr for the parent's waves (planner/run-1)
    
    The side campaign's first plan, under the current schemas: modules.json,
    schedule.json (schema 6) and dependencies.json, all new. It plans what
    libgit2-crustify's next waves reach through this wrapper and it lacks,
    _IO_FILE, fprintf and stderr, and records what landed before any schedule.
    
    Added, modules.json (link unit libc, at c/ ef321e23c2, glibc-2.39):
    - 0 time/bits/types/struct_tm.h, frozen: the header module Tm landed in
      (b7d01b0), kept as it landed.
    - 1 csu/errno-loc.c, frozen: __errno_location, with stdlib/errno.h's
      declaration and errno macro (787a802). csu/ is the TU Linux compiles
      (sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/Makefile, subdir csu); nptl/errno-loc.c only
      includes it.
    - 2 libio/genops.c: _IO_FILE, with libio/bits/types/struct_FILE.h (less
      _IO_codecvt and _IO_wide_data, the wide-stream TUs'), FILE.h, __FILE.h
      and stdio.h's __uflow and __overflow. genops.c implements the generic
      lifecycle every stream goes through (_IO_no_init, _IO_link_in,
      _IO_un_link, _IO_default_finish) and its buffer operations; iofopen.c
      and iofclose.c only allocate and free it, fileops.c is one stream kind.
    - 3 stdio-common/fprintf.c: fprintf, with its stdio.h declaration.
    - 4 libio/stdio.c: stdin, stdout and stderr, with their declarations and
      the C89 self-alias macros.
    As a wrap campaign over the system's libc, the decomposition holds the TUs
    that own a scoped entity and what their public signatures reach, and the
    dependency records are that signature graph's: fprintf.c and stdio.c each
    depend on genops.c for _IO_FILE (1 and 3 edges). Counters are counted from
    c/ by hand (definitions at column 0, nonblank noncomment lines less
    preprocessor directives, the installed configuration's branches).
    
    dependencies.json: no library. glibc's modules use none from outside the
    tree, so no route, candidate or wrapper applies, and no crustify-rs
    wrapper is needed by these waves.
    
    schedule.json:
    - waves 0 (struct_tm.h: tm) and 1 (errno-loc.c: __errno_location), done:
      recorded as landed, each one done wrap batch whose commits touched its
      home (b7d01b0 ea38101 8220840; 787a802), at the task message's request.
    - appended, todo: wave 2 (genops.c: _IO_FILE, typedef FILE, no
      field_users), wave 3 (fprintf.c: fprintf) and wave 4 (stdio.c: stderr),
      3 and 4 depending on 2 and free to run at once. No wave re-planned.
    What the waves offer the parent's uses:
    - _IO_FILE is bound opaque: no consumer touches a field, and none opens or
      closes a stream (each FILE * is the C's, or stderr), so it gets borrowed
      handles only, no owner, and fopen/fclose are not scheduled. glibc locks
      every stream operation, which the binder confirms before a shared handle
      writes.
    - fprintf is bound through a fixed-arity form, as binding-symbols'
      Variadics rule gives it: the formatted message, passed to fprintf(stream,
      "%s", message), the count or errno's io::Error returned. Every
      conversion the parents use (%s %c %d %p %02x, ffmpeg's %08x %0.3f) is
      formatted in Rust, and the text lands in the stream's FILE buffer, which
      the remaining C shares. vfprintf is not planned.
    - stderr is bound as a 'static shared handle: no C of either parent
      writes it, and its storage (_IO_2_1_stderr_) is static.
    The parent's waves: 188 and 189 (git2/src/cli/opt.c: spec_name_fprint,
    cli_opt_status_fprint) need _IO_FILE and fprintf; 194 (libgit2/deps/
    llhttp/api.c: llhttp__debug) needs fprintf and stderr. What waves 2 to 4
    plan for FILE serves ffmpeg-crustify's libavformat/dump.c too, whose
    av_hex_dump and av_pkt_dump2 write a caller's FILE * with fprintf.
    
    Crates left out of the rust_equivalent records: those that bind or
    reimplement libc, which modules-schema keeps out as alternatives to the
    campaign: libc, nix, rustix, relibc; errno (binds __errno_location);
    cstream 0.1.4 (borrowed and owned FILE streams over libc's stdio, with an
    io::Write over fwrite; no stdin/stdout/stderr, errors as (), last released
    2024-05-20); libc-stdhandle 0.1.0 (raw FILE * of the std streams, 2017);
    libc-print 0.5.0 (println over write(2), no FILE); printf-compat 0.5.0
    (reimplements printf's formatting). time 0.3.55 and chrono 0.4.45 are
    listed for struct_tm.h, partial.
    
    wavefront has no database over glibc here: nothing was queried, and no
    wavefront artifact is written; the entities, edges and counts were read
    from c/ and the parents' records.
    
    Reports: no plan correction (no earlier planner run). Proposal filed:
    crustify/evolution/plan-from-landings-before-a-schedule, open.
    
    Co-Authored-By: crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>

=== bindgen-opaque-allowlist-kind
# The raw bindings' allowlist can keep a type opaque that its routines take only by pointer

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-3/batch-1/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer). It is an
improvement to the spec and to the `-sys` build script it specifies, both owned by other
roles, so it is proposed.

## Signal

A rule worked around (`evolution` §2). The module pass's regression test needs
`register_printf_specifier` (`<printf.h>`). Allowlisting it, as wave 3's batch did for the
stream routines its tests call, pulls in `struct printf_info` through the handler types,
with its bit-fields. Regenerating `libc-sys/src/bindings.rs` grew it by 1295 lines,
almost all of them bindgen's `__BindgenBitfieldUnit` and `printf_info`'s accessors. The
test passes the struct on only by pointer. The run reverted the change and declared the
routine in its fixture, `tests/fixtures/stream_unit.rs`, with `*const c_void` for the
struct. That keeps a raw declaration outside the raw bindings, which the conventions do
not provide for.

`bindgen` §2 (allowlists) and the build script's `allowlist.txt` take three kinds,
`function`, `type` and `var` (`libc-sys/build.rs`). They cannot ask for bindgen's
`opaque_type`, which would generate `printf_info` as a sized blob of a few lines.

## Destination

- The spec: `bindgen`'s allowlist rules.
- The `-sys` build script it specifies: an `opaque <regex>` kind in `allowlist.txt`,
  mapped to `Builder::opaque_type`.

## Change

=== disclose-scope-for-the-campaigns-own-crate
# A disclosure goes to a project outside the campaign, never to the campaign's own crate

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-3/batch-1/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer). The change
is to the reviewing skill, which the reviewer evolves. It needs a review by another run, so
it is proposed.

## Signal

A rule worked out by hand that a skill should have stated (`evolution` §2). `reviewing`
§3.12 asks for a `disclosure.md` "beside each report that the user can send to the
affected project's maintainers unchanged". Where a review runs `disclose`, every objective
being on when a task names none, it does not say who the affected project is when the
defect lies in the crate the campaign itself generates. That crate has no maintainers but
the user, and the review fixes the defect itself under `fix`. Two module passes worked
this out by hand, alike:

- glibc-crustify `wave-2/batch-1/run-1` (`libio/genops.c`) filed three reports in
  `glibc-bindings` with no disclosure, and said nothing of it;
- this run (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`) filed two. One,
  `contracts/ffi_import/print-locks-a-stream-without-a-lock`, rests on glibc behaviour:
  `flockfile` dereferences the NULL lock of the stream glibc hands a printf handler. The
  run had to judge whether that is a glibc defect to disclose. It is not: glibc's routines
  skip the lock on that stream by design, and before 2.37 the helper stream of an
  unbuffered stream had none either. So it wrote no disclosure.

## Destination

The spec: `reviewing` §3.12, Disclosure.

=== doc-alias-equal-to-name
# conventions: no `doc(alias)` where the Rust item's name is the anchor's path

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-4/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer): a defect in
the spec that does not block the batch, proposed, since `conventions` is not the binder's to
evolve.

## Signal

A rule the compiler refuses (`evolution` §2, "a rule an agent works around").
`conventions`' Anchors section asks every stand-in for two attributes, the doc-comment
anchor and `#[doc(alias = "<path>")]`. Its Naming section keeps a C name where it is already
idiomatic Rust, as a global or function named in `snake_case` is. Wave 4 binds the global
`stderr` as `pub fn stderr() -> FileRef<'static>` (`src/libc/libio/stdio.rs`), and rustc
rejects the alias as an error, with workspace warnings denied or not:

```text
error: `#[doc(alias = "stderr"]` is the same as the item's name
  --> src/libc/libio/stdio.rs:46:19
```

The alias serves a consumer who searches the documentation for the C name, and the item's
own name already serves that search. The same holds for any C function or global whose
`snake_case` name the Rust keeps, such as wave 3's `fprintf` if its fixed-arity form keeps
the name.

## Destination

The spec: `conventions` §3, Anchors. And a tool: `ffimap api`'s `anchors.without_alias`
(`docs/api.md` §2, at `9aa2ef1`), which lists the item as an anchor without its alias:

=== errno-failure-without-errno
# A failure that sets no `errno` is not reported as the stale one

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-3/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer). It is a gap
in the spec and in a tool's documentation. It did not block the batch, so it is proposed.

A rule worked out by hand that a skill should have stated (`evolution` §2), and one that
the tool's documentation leads a binder wrong on. `binding-symbols`' Functions section reads
a failure from "error state the library keeps beside the call, read immediately after it".
ffibox's `docs/patterns.md` maps "`-1` for failure, the error in `errno`" to
`status::errno`, which returns `io::Error::last_os_error()` on a `-1`

=== ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking
# ffibox: the shared seam's contract for a C object that locks itself

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-2/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy: a documentation defect in ffibox that does not block the batch,
proposed.

## Signal

Two ffibox documents disagree (`evolution` §2, "skills that contradict each other", here a
tool's docs). `CCell::ref_from_ptr` (`src/traits.rs`, at `9c22a73`), which
`CRefSeam::from_ptr` forwards to, requires that "nothing may write it while the handle
lives except through a `Mut` derived from the same borrow". `docs/ownership.md`'s
shared-and-mutable table puts "routines that lock internally" on `FooRef`. The macro's own
`CCell` safety comment, "`$rf` has no write operation", says the same as the trait.

A C object that serializes its own state, such as glibc's `FILE`, whose every stdio
routine writes its buffer under the stream's recursive lock, cannot meet the trait's
wording. C writes such an object while a `FooRef` lives, on another thread too, and that
is exactly what the table allows. Wave 2 of glibc-crustify binds `FILE` opaque, as
`File`/`FileRef`, and states the contract for a stream on the type
(`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`): the stream stays open for `'a`, and whatever else writes it
does so under its lock, while the handle reads nothing without the lock. That is the
table's meaning, but it is not the trait's text.

## Destination

ffibox: `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s `# Safety` section, and the `CCell` safety comment
`define_ctype!` emits.

whole of its access. A `Sync` that relied on the stream's locking mode would rest on data
the native code can change, which `binding`'s Safe boundary section forbids.

content.content:
# libc's wrapper writes text, not the bytes C streams carry

Status: `open`.

## Signal

A route the plan recommends that holds for an entity's state but not for its values: an
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks part of it.

## Evidence

`wave-186/batch-4/run-1` (`git2/src/cli/opt.c`) ported `cli_opt_status_fprint`, which writes
an argument parse's error to the `FILE *` the CLI's C hands it (`stderr`, from `main.c` and
`opt_usage.c`). `_IO_FILE` and `fprintf` take the `crustify-campaign` route, which holds: the
CLI's remaining C writes the same stream, so the export writes through glibc-bindings'
`FileRef` (pinned at `1e60130`), whose only write is `FileRef::print(&str)` (and `write_fmt`),
one locked `fprintf(stream, "%s", text)`.

The message holds the user's argument, `unknown option: <arg>`, and the specs' names, as C
strings, which C writes as their bytes. An argument need not be UTF-8: `argv` holds whatever
the shell passed. `&str` cannot carry it, so the export's `FileWriter` (an `io::Write` over
`FileRef`, in `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`) writes such a piece through
`String::from_utf8_lossy`: `--caf\xe9` comes out as `--caf\u{fffd}`, where C writes the byte.
The inline test `ffi_import::equiv_priv::the_export_writes_what_c_writes` asserts both sides of
that departure. The native API, `OptRef::write_status(&mut impl io::Write, …)`, writes the
bytes exactly; only the export departs, and only for bytes that are not UTF-8.

`opt_usage.c` (`cli_opt_usage_fprint`, `cli_opt_help_fprint`) and `progress.c`, which the
plan routes the same way, print the same strings and will meet the same gap.

## Destination

The glibc-crustify side campaign: `fprintf.c`'s wrapper, `FileRef`. As the `dependencies`
skill's Side campaigns section has it, the parent reports the entity its wrapper lacks and the
side campaign wraps it.

## Change

Not made: the side campaign's. A byte-exact write beside `print`, such as
`FileRef::print_c_str(&self, text: &CStr) -> io::Result<usize>`, the same locked
`fprintf(stream, "%s", text)` over a string that is already NUL-terminated, with `print`'s
errors and lock. `FileWriter` then writes each piece through it, with a `CString` of the piece
(which holds no NUL: the pieces are C strings and literals), and its departure goes. It is
needed before `opt.c` switches from C, at its integration.

## Validation

None yet: the change is the side campaign's. The equivalence test above turns into an exact
comparison once the export writes through it.

## Review

None yet.

# `File`'s contract for a borrowed stream trusts glibc's own stdio routines to hold its lock, which they skip on a `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` stream

- **item**: `st::_IO_FILE` / `tdf::FILE`, bound as `File` with `FileRef` and `FileMut`,
  `src/libc/libio/genops.rs`: the contract the type's documentation gives
  `FileRef::from_ptr` for a stream, on which the `Send` and `Sync` assertions of `File` and
  `FileRef` rest
- **affected commit**: `915f5a4` (wave 2, batch 0)
- **objective**: `contracts`, of the `ffi_import` region. The obligation is incorrect. It
  names glibc's own stdio routines as writers that meet it, and on some streams they do not.
  No safe path reaches undefined behaviour today, since nothing bound on `FileRef` reads or
  writes the stream yet. So there is no Rust reproducer. The evidence is glibc's source, and
  the C demonstration below.

## What is wrong

`File`'s documentation states the contract a caller of `FileRef::from_ptr` keeps for a
stream:

> the pointer is NULL or an open stream that stays open for the handle's lifetime, `fclose`
> included, and whatever else writes it while the handle lives does so under its lock, as
> glibc's own stdio routines do.

`FileRef`'s `Sync` relies on that last clause. Every operation bound on `FileRef` holds the
stream's lock, taken with `flockfile`, so two Rust operations exclude each other. A Rust
operation excludes a C writer only if that writer takes the same lock. The clause tells the
caller that glibc's own routines do. They do so only while the stream's locking is internal:

- the locking stdio routines lock through the `_IO_flockfile` macro, which is a no-op when
  the stream carries `_IO_USER_LOCK` (`c/libio/libio.h:282-285`), and
  `__fsetlocking(fp, FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER)` sets that flag (`c/libio/__fsetlocking.c:30-32`);
- the walkers of every open stream lock each one with the same macro: `fflush(NULL)`
  (`_IO_flush_all`, `c/libio/genops.c:698`), `_IO_flush_all_linebuffered` (`:734`) and
  `exit`'s `_IO_unbuffer_all` (`:785`). So on such a stream they write without the lock too,
  from whichever thread calls them;
- the `_unlocked` routines never take it, on any stream.

The type's own *Shared* paragraph says the first and third of these. The contract's last
clause contradicts it. A caller who reads that clause and checks only that the C writing
the stream is glibc's (`fprintf`, `fputs`, `fflush`) honours the contract as written. But
it can hand over a stream that C has set to `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` and writes on another
thread without `flockfile`. Once wave 3 binds a write on `FileRef`, that write and C's would
race on the stream's buffer.

## Evidence

The C side of the scenario, on the host's glibc (`Ubuntu GLIBC 2.39-0ubuntu8.9`). One thread
holds the stream's lock, as a Rust operation on `FileRef` does. Another thread writes the
stream with glibc's `fputs`, as C that stays C would. The program records whether the write
finished while the lock was still held:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdio_ext.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
static FILE *fp; static atomic_int wrote;
static void *writer(void *a) { (void)a; fputs("x", fp); atomic_store(&wrote, 1); return 0; }
static int run(int mode) {
  fp = fopen("/dev/null", "w"); atomic_store(&wrote, 0);
======
# `stderr()` lends a `FileRef<'static>` from safe code, on assumptions about the program's C that the crate cannot check

- **item**: `glb::stderr`, bound as `stderr() -> FileRef<'static>`,
  `src/libc/libio/stdio.rs`: the two `// SAFETY:` justifications of its `ffi_import` body
  and the safe signature they let it keep
- **affected commit**: `2a792a8` (wave 4, batch 0)
- **objective**: `contracts`, of the `ffi_import` region. A safe function discharges
  `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract for the `'static` lifetime by assuming what the whole
  program's C does with a variable glibc lets it set. The contract breaks through safe
  code. The reproducer below shows a heap-use-after-free under ASan.

## What is wrong

`stderr()` is safe and returns `FileRef<'static>`. Its body reads the global `stderr` and
borrows the stream it names with `FileRef::from_ptr`, whose contract for a stream
(`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`, `File`'s documentation, as `6e892ea` corrected it) is:

> the pointer is NULL or an open stream that stays open for the handle's lifetime, `fclose`
> included, and every other access to it while the handle lives, C's or Rust's, on any
> thread, holds its lock.

For `'static`, the function discharges this with assumptions about the program, which its
doc lists. No code assigns `stderr` while another thread may read it. Nothing passes its
stream to `fclose` or to a failing `freopen`. Its locking stays internal. The doc and the
batch's commit message justify these by what glibc's own routines and the C of the two
parent campaigns do. They do not follow from anything the crate or the C contract
guarantees:

- glibc's `stderr` is a variable a program may set. Its manual (`c/manual/stdio.texi:115-122`)
  says so: "In the GNU C Library, `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` are normal variables which
  you can set just like any others." It gives `fclose (stdout); stdout = fopen (…);` as
  the way to redirect a standard stream.
- A stream so opened is heap memory that `fclose` frees. `_IO_new_fclose` ends in
  `_IO_deallocate_file` (`c/libio/iofclose.c:74`), which spares only `_IO_2_1_stdin_`,
  `_IO_2_1_stdout_` and `_IO_2_1_stderr_` and frees every other stream
  (`c/libio/libioP.h:948-958`). Even `_IO_2_1_stderr_` is closed by `fclose`, and C11
  7.21.3p4 leaves a closed stream's pointer indeterminate.
- The handle is `Copy`, `Send` and `'static`, so safe code may keep it anywhere: in a
  `static`, as the batch's own `ub_safe` test `the_handle_outlives_every_scope` does, or on
  a detached thread. C's own `fprintf (stderr, …)` reads the variable at each call. A kept
  Rust handle does not, so a program that redirects its standard error stream is correct C
  and still leaves the handle dangling.

`glibc-bindings` is a library. It is linked into programs whose C it cannot see, and the
parents' C is not all of that C either: libgit2 is itself a library. `binding-symbols`'
Globals section binds a global by its C accesses. A global that is neither immutable after
initialization nor synchronized by C is "otherwise mutable", and gets `unsafe` accessors
that exclude concurrent access. ffibox's goals (`docs/goals.md`, G9 and G10) exclude use
after free through lifetimes, and make adopting a pointer `unsafe`, "an unknown fact
selects[ing] the more restrictive primitive". The safe `'static` signature does neither.

it can hand over a stream that C has set to `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` and writes on another
thread without `flockfile`. Once wave 3 binds a write on `FileRef`, that write and C's would
race on the stream's buffer.

## Evidence

The C side of the scenario, on the host's glibc (`Ubuntu GLIBC 2.39-0ubuntu8.9`). One thread
holds the stream's lock, as a Rust operation on `FileRef` does. Another thread writes the
stream with glibc's `fputs`, as C that stays C would. The program records whether the write
finished while the lock was still held:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdio_ext.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
static FILE *fp; static atomic_int wrote;
static void *writer(void *a) { (void)a; fputs("x", fp); atomic_store(&wrote, 1); return 0; }
static int run(int mode) {
  fp = fopen("/dev/null", "w"); atomic_store(&wrote, 0);
======
# `stderr()` lends a `FileRef<'static>` from safe code, on assumptions about the program's C that the crate cannot check

- **item**: `glb::stderr`, bound as `stderr() -> FileRef<'static>`,
  `src/libc/libio/stdio.rs`: the two `// SAFETY:` justifications of its `ffi_import` body
  and the safe signature they let it keep
- **affected commit**: `2a792a8` (wave 4, batch 0)
- **objective**: `contracts`, of the `ffi_import` region. A safe function discharges
  `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract for the `'static` lifetime by assuming what the whole
  program's C does with a variable glibc lets it set. The contract breaks through safe
  code. The reproducer below shows a heap-use-after-free under ASan.

## What is wrong

`stderr()` is safe and returns `FileRef<'static>`. Its body reads the global `stderr` and
borrows the stream it names with `FileRef::from_ptr`, whose contract for a stream
(`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`, `File`'s documentation, as `6e892ea` corrected it) is:

> the pointer is NULL or an open stream that stays open for the handle's lifetime, `fclose`
> included, and every other access to it while the handle lives, C's or Rust's, on any
> thread, holds its lock.

For `'static`, the function discharges this with assumptions about the program, which its
doc lists. No code assigns `stderr` while another thread may read it. Nothing passes its
stream to `fclose` or to a failing `freopen`. Its locking stays internal. The doc and the
batch's commit message justify these by what glibc's own routines and the C of the two
parent campaigns do. They do not follow from anything the crate or the C contract
guarantees:

- glibc's `stderr` is a variable a program may set. Its manual (`c/manual/stdio.texi:115-122`)
  says so: "In the GNU C Library, `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` are normal variables which
  you can set just like any others." It gives `fclose (stdout); stdout = fopen (…);` as
  the way to redirect a standard stream.
- A stream so opened is heap memory that `fclose` frees. `_IO_new_fclose` ends in
  `_IO_deallocate_file` (`c/libio/iofclose.c:74`), which spares only `_IO_2_1_stdin_`,
  `_IO_2_1_stdout_` and `_IO_2_1_stderr_` and frees every other stream
  (`c/libio/libioP.h:948-958`). Even `_IO_2_1_stderr_` is closed by `fclose`, and C11
  7.21.3p4 leaves a closed stream's pointer indeterminate.
- The handle is `Copy`, `Send` and `'static`, so safe code may keep it anywhere: in a
  `static`, as the batch's own `ub_safe` test `the_handle_outlives_every_scope` does, or on
  a detached thread. C's own `fprintf (stderr, …)` reads the variable at each call. A kept
  Rust handle does not, so a program that redirects its standard error stream is correct C
  and still leaves the handle dangling.

`glibc-bindings` is a library. It is linked into programs whose C it cannot see, and the
parents' C is not all of that C either: libgit2 is itself a library. `binding-symbols`'
Globals section binds a global by its C accesses. A global that is neither immutable after
initialization nor synchronized by C is "otherwise mutable", and gets `unsafe` accessors
that exclude concurrent access. ffibox's goals (`docs/goals.md`, G9 and G10) exclude use
after free through lifetimes, and make adopting a pointer `unsafe`, "an unknown fact
selects[ing] the more restrictive primitive". The safe `'static` signature does neither.

content.content:
---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, the record of what landed and how evolution itself evolves. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not
filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.

A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
code, and is filed with its reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
  it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.

## 11. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not
filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.

A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
code, and is filed with its reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
  it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.

## 11. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

After the list of access disciplines, add:

> The accesses that decide are those the C declaration's contract allows, not those the
> campaign's C makes: a global the library documents as one a program may set, such as
> libc's standard streams, `environ` or `optarg`, is otherwise mutable however the code
> the campaign sees uses it, since the crate cannot see every program it is linked into.
> Where it holds a pointer, what it points to may be freed by the C that reassigns it, so
> a safe accessor never lends what it names beyond the call: the accessor is `unsafe`,
> its caller vouching for the lifetime it chooses, or a safe operation reads the global
> and uses what it names within one call, as the C expression does, holding the lock C
> takes there.

## Validation

The rerun is the module pass's fix (`wave-4/batch-1`). Under the rule, `stderr` is bound
as `unsafe fn stderr<'a>() -> FileRef<'a>`. The reproducer's safe step then fails to
compile (`E0133`), which `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/stdio_stderr_is_lent_by_no_safe_code.rs`
keeps. The workspace's tests pass plain and under ASan and TSan, and Miri passes per test
binary.

## Review

Not reviewed.

`funlockfile` (`stdio-common/flockfile.c`, `stdio-common/funlockfile.c`, declared in

binding needs them. They could also be bound privately inside `fprintf`'s module, as the
lock its one call takes, with no public API of their own.

## Change

Planner run 2 adds the two functions as items wave 3 reaches. The fixed-arity form stays
as planned: `flockfile(stream)`, `fprintf(stream, "%s", message)`, `funlockfile(stream)`,
with the count returned, or `errno`'s `io::Error` on a negative return.

## Validation

Wave 3's binder confirmed it from `fprintf`'s analysis, and the assistant's task message
settled the destination: the two routines are raw bindings in `fprintf.rs`'s `ffi_import`,
allowlisted, with no safe API. `FileRef::print` holds the lock from before `fprintf` to
after `errno` is read. Two unit tests show that the lock is what serializes the writes
(`tests/unit_pub/fprintf.rs`). `writes_from_threads_never_interleave` shares one handle
among 8 threads on a `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` stream. It passes, and with the binding's
`flockfile` and `funlockfile` removed it fails three runs in three with interleaved lines
(an `open_memstream` stream aborts in glibc instead).
`print_waits_for_the_lock_on_a_stream_locked_by_its_caller` passes, and with them removed
it sees the waiting thread's text written first. No consumer of the parent campaigns needs
the lock routines as API of their own: `cli_opt_status_fprint`, `spec_name_fprint` and
`llhttp__debug` each make one `fprintf` per message.

## Review

Not reviewed.

None yet: the rules are what the run did by hand. A second planner run of this campaign,
or the first plan of another side campaign with landings before its schedule (zlib-,
openssl- and pcre2-crustify have no plan either), would show whether the wording leads it
to the same records.

## Review

Not reviewed.

## Record

Recurrence signal: a planner run that schedules again an item that landed before its
campaign's schedule, or that emits modules a wrap campaign's public signatures do not reach.
=====

## Destination

The spec: `binding-symbols` §2, Globals.

## Change

After the list of access disciplines, add:

> The accesses that decide are those the C declaration's contract allows, not those the
> campaign's C makes: a global the library documents as one a program may set, such as
> libc's standard streams, `environ` or `optarg`, is otherwise mutable however the code
> the campaign sees uses it, since the crate cannot see every program it is linked into.
> Where it holds a pointer, what it points to may be freed by the C that reassigns it, so
> a safe accessor never lends what it names beyond the call: the accessor is `unsafe`,
> its caller vouching for the lifetime it chooses, or a safe operation reads the global
> and uses what it names within one call, as the C expression does, holding the lock C
> takes there.

## Validation

The rerun is the module pass's fix (`wave-4/batch-1`). Under the rule, `stderr` is bound
as `unsafe fn stderr<'a>() -> FileRef<'a>`. The reproducer's safe step then fails to
compile (`E0133`), which `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/stdio_stderr_is_lent_by_no_safe_code.rs`
keeps. The workspace's tests pass plain and under ASan and TSan, and Miri passes per test
binary.

## Review

Not reviewed.
====
A campaign artifact: `modules.json` and `schedule.json`, the planner's. `flockfile` and
`funlockfile` (`stdio-common/flockfile.c`, `stdio-common/funlockfile.c`, declared in
`libio/stdio.h`) join the plan ahead of wave 3, or in its batch, since wave 3's `fprintf`
binding needs them. They could also be bound privately inside `fprintf`'s module, as the
lock its one call takes, with no public API of their own.

## Change

Planner run 2 adds the two functions as items wave 3 reaches. The fixed-arity form stays
as planned: `flockfile(stream)`, `fprintf(stream, "%s", message)`, `funlockfile(stream)`,
with the count returned, or `errno`'s `io::Error` on a negative return.

## Validation

Wave 3's binder confirmed it from `fprintf`'s analysis, and the assistant's task message
settled the destination: the two routines are raw bindings in `fprintf.rs`'s `ffi_import`,
allowlisted, with no safe API. `FileRef::print` holds the lock from before `fprintf` to
after `errno` is read. Two unit tests show that the lock is what serializes the writes
(`tests/unit_pub/fprintf.rs`). `writes_from_threads_never_interleave` shares one handle
among 8 threads on a `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` stream. It passes, and with the binding's
`flockfile` and `funlockfile` removed it fails three runs in three with interleaved lines
(an `open_memstream` stream aborts in glibc instead).

it sees the waiting thread's text written first. No consumer of the parent campaigns needs
the lock routines as API of their own: `cli_opt_status_fprint`, `spec_name_fprint` and
`llhttp__debug` each make one `fprintf` per message.

## Review

Not reviewed.

description: "How a scheduled C symbol becomes a safe Rust binding, binding's symbol route: functions and what their signatures carry, globals, function pointers, macros and lifecycle strategies. Read before binding any symbol, and when reviewing bindings."

# Binding symbols

How a scheduled C symbol becomes a safe Rust binding: the symbol route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section and reaches the types
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md) binds. [`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md) starts from it.

## 1. Functions

A function is bound as a `pub fn`; it is a `pub unsafe fn` only when no safe type-level
contract can express its caller obligation. Its FFI call, and the raw pointers it
reconstructs for it, sit in its module's `ffi_import` region, as the
[conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes.

Its signature follows the analysis's findings, each argument and return taking the safe
form of what it names:

- **Out-parameters.** A pointer the function only writes through, to hand back a result,
  is part of the return, several of them a tuple, present only in the outcome in which the
  function writes it.
- **Buffers.** A pointer and the count that bounds it are one slice, the count taken from
  it; a buffer the function fills returns the part it filled.
- **Strings.** A NUL-terminated string the function borrows for the call is a borrowed C
  string, or the Rust string or path type of the encoding the analysis establishes,
  converted at the call, an interior NUL rejected before it. A returned string is a borrow
  tied to what keeps it alive, or an owner over its releaser where the caller frees it.
- **Nullability.** A nullable pointer is an `Option`.
- **Errors.** A function that can fail returns a `Result`, its failure read from the error
  convention the analysis establishes: a status return, a sentinel return, or error state
  the library keeps beside the call, read immediately after it, before another call into
  the library can replace it. A return that reports only success is not returned, and an
  outcome its C callers treat as ordinary, such as an exhausted iteration or an absent
  entry, is part of the success value. Each error convention has one error type, carrying
  what the convention reports, `errno`'s being `std::io::Error`.
- **Variadics.** A variadic function is bound through fixed-arity forms: one that formats
  its arguments takes the formatted message, passed to a `"%s"` format, and any other is

A method is emitted in an `impl T` block on the type it implements, taking `&self` or
`&mut self` as its first argument. A free function stays free.

## 2. Globals

A global is bound as a `'static` borrow, never as an owner, its value taking the safe form
its type takes in a signature, as [Functions](#1-functions) describes. Its access
discipline follows from every C access:

- immutable after initialization: a shared handle;
- synchronized by C: the matching safe synchronization (an atomic, or guards handing out
  the shared or exclusive handle under the lock), never discarding a lock's status;
- otherwise mutable: `unsafe` accessors that exclude concurrent access, reported as such;
- thread-local: a handle borrowed for a closure on the current thread, neither `Send` nor
  `Sync`.

A lock counts only if every access takes it and it rejects same-thread re-entry. A global
C sets up in a routine, rather than in its definition, is reached through the safe API only
once that routine has run, however the binding ensures it.

## 3. Function pointers

A function pointer is bound from its declaration and every site that calls it or supplies
it, a function assigned to it or passed as it. One a typedef declares is named after its
typedef; one written inline is named after the site that declares it, the field,

name: binding
description: "How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding: the safe boundary every binding keeps, and the routes binding-types and binding-symbols give types and symbols. Read before binding any item, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

projected with `addr_of!`, `addr_of_mut!`, `&raw const` or `&raw mut`, never with
`&(*p).field` or `&mut (*p).field`.

Each kind of field is expressed as follows:

- An owned-reference field has a replacement setter that drops the old owner, an owning
  getter that leaves the field valid, and a shared borrowed getter.
- A by-value wrapped field has a shared or mutable handle over the projected place.
- A stored borrow without an expressible lifetime has an unsafe setter whose caller
  contract carries the referent-lifetime obligation.
- Statically known owned and borrowed cases have distinct wrapper forms, with a shared
  trait where useful.
- A runtime ownership flag has separately checked owned and borrowed operations.
- A union field and its discriminator are one accessor of a tagged Rust enum, as
  [Unions](#5-unions) describes.
- Scalar and array variants have separate typed forms.
- A type-erased field takes a generic element type when it is known, and the discovered
  untyped lifetime strategy otherwise.
most authoritative: the formats and standards the library implements, its documentation,
what its own test suites assert, and its maintainers' stated intent. A finding cites what
the behaviour departs from. Where the C departs from it too, the defect is not copied into
the Rust, and the finding records the C's. A leak, a deadlock or a panic on valid input
departs from nearly every specification.

### 3.6 Ergonomics (`ergonomics`)

Public API that is harder to use than it needs to be: its names, its conversions, its
iterators, builders or defaults where the C takes long argument lists, and the standard
traits its types lack. An item's safe API is fixed by the first batch that gives it one, a
wrap included, so its ergonomics are reviewed there.

Ported implementation that transliterates its C rather than using Rust's own means: index
loops where iterators fit, status codes where `Result` and `?` fit, lengths and releases
carried by hand where ownership carries them.
